opener.heading: Week 48: Kitchen Helpers 👩‍🍳
about: Seven days in the kitchen, and the same question sits under all of them: what does a tool do that her own two hands cannot? She races a masher against a fork and counts both, cuts her own noodles and hangs them over a chair back, whisks four egg whites into half a bowl of foam, fills one cup with four different things, and seasons a bowl of tomatoes a pinch at a time. Wednesday she gets a drawer of her own with eight things in it. Thursday she cooks the dinner and the house sits down to eat what she made.

Thanksgiving was yesterday, so Friday opens with a refrigerator full of leftovers and she rules on every one of them before it goes in the pot. December arrives on Wednesday, and the frost has been through the garden overnight, so she walks the beds naming what it flattened and what shrugged it off. Her noodles, her muffins and her cheese straws all come back on Thursday as parts of a dinner nobody helped her design.
azlyn: A tool does one job faster than her hands. She works thirty counts by hand, thirty counts with the tool, and calls the winner herself.
One cup holds one cup. Rice, water, sugar and cotton balls all fill it to the same line, and Monday she tests that against a scale with flour.
Dough answers to her hands. Kneading, rolling it thin enough to see her fingers through, cutting strips, twisting pastry two ways at once.
Seasoning is a loop. One pinch, one stir, one taste, and a splash of water to pull it back when she goes too far.
Everything in a kitchen lives somewhere. She empties a cabinet, counts it, sorts it, and draws the labels that say where it all goes back.
you: Machines that make hard work easier are only obvious at this scale
Laying the track is planning, and it's harder than driving on it
Air is invisible, and she needs to feel it push before she'll believe in it
Pumping a tire is the first time she'll feel her own strength do something useful
Finishing a week by using everything she made beats one more new thing
The moon changing shape is the first thing she'll notice that she can't touch
Distance is the part of space that nobody tells her about
shopping: Self-rising flour, 1 lb, or more all-purpose flour plus baking powder
Vinegar, and lemon juice if you have it
Rolled oats, 2 lb, the cheapest bag in the store
Large dried pasta shapes, a handful
Hard cheese for grating, a 12 oz block
Salad and vegetables for Thursday, hers to pick where you can manage it
Rosemary, one sprig off a bush, or a jar of dried
Puff pastry, 1 sheet, into the refrigerator Tuesday night
Leftover cooked vegetables and meat from yesterday
Garlic press, or a wide knife to press with
Fine-mesh sieve or strainer, 2, one of them hers from Wednesday
Balloon whisk, plus a small whisk for her drawer
Jam jar with a lid, for Thursday's dressing and as the stand-in if there is no whisk in the house
Rolling pin, or a clean bottle
Wooden spoons, 2, one of them hers
Kitchen scale, or a second measuring cup
Pastry brush, or a teaspoon in its place
Mixing bowls, 3, one of them metal or glass
Pitchers, 3, one a small plastic one for her drawer
Funnel, or the top half of a cut plastic bottle
Dish towels, 5, one of them hers from Wednesday
Salt shaker she can fill herself
Forks, 2 for the mashing test and enough more for the table
Tin or airtight container, and a paper bag
Trash bag, plus 2 grocery bags for out-of-date food and the food bank
Hook or peg for her apron, with screws, or adhesive pads instead
Screwdriver to match the screws, if you go the screw route
Step stool she can stand on at the counter
Card stock, or an empty cereal box
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 17 months this week. He kicks a ball with a real swing, carries things the whole length of a walk, and hands them over on purpose when he gets there. Two-word pairs are arriving: more that, my one. He wants a job whenever he can see one going.

days.title: The Tools That Do the Work
days.prepTonight: Boil four extra potatoes with tonight's dinner and leave them in the fridge, then tip the tool drawer into a tray on the table.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Tool Drawer on the Floor

opening.title: The Tool Line-Up
opening.need: the tray of kitchen tools · 1 sheet of paper · 1 marker.
steps: Tip the tray out and let her line every tool up in whatever order suits her. She will put the masher beside the whisk because they look like relatives, so leave it.
Point at six of them and ask what each one is for. Write her answers on the paper word for word, wrong ones included.
Ask which of them beats her own two hands. Do not answer. Tell her you are finding out at 9:15.

main.title: Masher Against Fork
materials: 1 garlic press, or the flat of a knife
Paper and a marker for the scores
steps: Dish towel flat on the table, three bowls on it, paper and marker alongside. Head the sheet HANDS and TOOL.
Two potatoes into the first bowl. She mashes one half with the two forks while you count thirty out loud, then the other half with the masher, same count. She calls the winner.
Break the other two open and push a lump of each through the garlic press, or squash them under the flat of a knife. They come out in threads.
Cheese into the second bowl: thirty counts of her fork down the cut face, then thirty with you holding the box grater and her pushing the block.
A cup of flour into the third bowl, thumped and shaken to get the lumps out. Hold the sieve over the same bowl for the second cup, then a finger in each side.
Read the sheet back. Ask which one tool she would keep if the rest went in a box.
main.tip: A count of thirty is the only fair test she can follow. Same count, same voice, both times.

outside.title: Cutting a Sprig of Rosemary
paras: Rosemary is one of the few things worth picking at the end of November, green and hard and smelling of itself. Find a bush: your own pot, a neighbor's front wall, the edge of the parking lot. Run her hand up a stem the wrong way and let her smell her palm. She snaps one sprig low down and carries it home for the pan at 1:00.

days.infant: Kreston is 17 months and kicks a ball, so he can send a saucepan lid the length of the kitchen floor. Hand him one while the mashing goes on. Two-word pairs are arriving: big spoon, that one. Say the tool names out loud as Azlyn tests them, and let him mouth the lid and a wooden spoon while the grater, the peeler and the can opener stay up on the table.

second.title: The Day-After Soup
second.intro: This afternoon she chooses what goes in the pan, and nobody overrules her.
materials: The rosemary sprig, or a pinch of dried herbs
steps: Everything out of the fridge onto the cutting board in a row. She goes along it saying in or out, and the carrots get left behind.
She cuts her pile with the butter knife and tears the meat with her fingers.
Crumble the bouillon cube into the pan with hot water and set it on the back burner. She adds her pieces a handful at a time from her step.
She stirs with the wooden spoon until it simmers, then strips the rosemary sprig in with a thumb and finger, or scatters a pinch of dried herbs.
Cool a spoonful on the back of the wooden spoon and let her taste. Ask what it needs. Salt, water and more time are the three real answers.
Twenty minutes on, she ladles it into the four bowls one at a time, your hand steadying the ladle.
She names the soup at the table and everyone uses the name. Bread torn, not sliced.
second.tip: Let her leave out something you would have put in. A soup she designed and half likes beats one you fixed behind her.

alternatives: Soup from a can, and she stirs and ladles.
Sandwiches to her design, same in-or-out row.
Wash the whole tool tray in a bowl of bubbles.
Sort the drawer by size and put it back her way.
outAgain: Playgroup, and let her tell somebody what a garlic press does
The park while it is light, which now means before half past four
The store for bread, and she carries the loaf
A walk to the mailbox before the light goes, counting front doors

aroundWorld.title: Noodles, Everywhere 🍜
paras: Flour and water turn up as noodles almost everywhere. Italian cooks roll sheets and cut tagliatelle, Japanese cooks work wheat into udon thick enough to chew, and in northern China a cook pulls one lump of dough into hundreds of strands by folding and stretching it, no knife involved. The oldest noodles anyone has dug up came out of the ground in China, made of millet, four thousand years ago.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Roll a rope of tomorrow's dough between your palms and pull it long. Hers snaps, and that break is the whole difficulty of hand-pulled noodles.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Chinese longevity noodles arrive in one unbroken strand, and cutting a birthday bowl of them is bad manners.

days.krestonPM: At 17 months he copies any hands he can see, so give him a wooden spoon and a cold empty pan at the far end of the kitchen while Azlyn works at the stovetop. He stirs nothing with commitment. At playgroup he goes for the ride-ons and the ball, and he minds now when another child takes one.

insight.headline: Machines that make hard work easier are only obvious at this scale.
paras: Azlyn cannot see what a car engine or a washing machine does for anybody. A masher she can see, because she has now done one job twice with her own arms and counted the same thirty both times. Children build the idea of a tool out of that: a task felt in the hands, then the same task handed to an object. The order matters, hands first and tool second. Once she has it, the drawer works as a set of answers to problems she recognizes, and she starts asking what the rest of the house is for. Those questions land because she asked them.

days.safety: A box grater takes knuckles off, so you hold it and she pushes the cheese. Take the grater, the peeler, the can opener and anything with a point out of the tray before it goes down on the floor, and leave her the spoons, the masher, the whisk and the measuring cups. Kreston mouths every tool he reaches at 17 months, so he works this one beside you or not at all. The soup pan goes on the back burner with the handle turned in, out of Kreston's reach at 17 months.

days.title: The Noodles She Cut
days.prepTonight: Measure 2 1/3 cups of flour into a bowl and stand it on the table with three eggs and the rolling pin, and pull a chair clear for drying.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: A Bowl Each, Built to Order

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: Wiping the Flour Off the Table

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: Drawing in Flour on the Baking Tray

opening.title: The Well in the Flour
opening.need: the measured flour · 3 eggs · a clear table or a big board.
steps: Tip the flour you measured out last night into one heap in the middle of the table and let her flatten the top with her palm.
She pushes a fist down through the middle, then walks her fingers round the inside until the walls stand up on their own.
Crack the eggs into her well one at a time while she watches for a leak. Leave it standing there until 9:15.

main.title: Hand-Cut Noodles
materials: 3 eggs, or 2/3 cup warm water (150 ml)
1 rolling pin, or a clean bottle
1 clean chair back or a coat hanger for drying
steps: She breaks the yolks with two fingers and pulls flour in from the walls until the middle turns to paste and then to a lump.
Knead in turns for ten minutes: heel of the hand, push, fold, quarter turn. Hers is a squash rather than a push. Rest the ball under a dish towel.
Flour the board hard and roll it out with the rolling pin or the bottle, thin enough to see her fingers through.
Flour the top, fold the sheet over three times, and let her cut across the folds with the butter knife. Fat ones, thin ones, one enormous one.
Shake the strips loose. Half go over the chair back or the coat hanger, the rest coil into nests on the second dish towel on the baking tray.
Leave them to dry until 1:00 and keep her out of them.
main.tip: Flour anything sticky, add water by the teaspoon to anything cracking, and let her decide which it needs.

outside.title: Where the Steam Comes Out
paras: Cold air makes every warm thing on the street visible. Walk the block hunting steam: furnace vents on house walls, a dryer vent, the bakery door. She breathes out hard and finds her own. Hold her hand near a vent so she feels wet warm air, then say the word steam once and leave it with her.

days.infant: Kreston is 17 months and wants whatever Azlyn has, so give him a fistful of all-purpose flour and a spoon on his tray while the kneading goes on. None of the egg dough goes near him. He drags one finger through the flour forty times.

second.title: A Bowl Each, Built to Order
second.intro: Six bowls go down the middle of the table and everybody builds their own dinner.
steps: Six small bowls in a row down the middle of the table. She fills every one and nobody else touches them.
You peel the carrot into ribbons with the vegetable peeler and she coils them into the first bowl.
She tears the green onion or chives into the second and pulls the cooked chicken or ham into shreds for the third.
Boil the 4 eggs eight minutes, cool them under the tap, and she picks the shells off into the fourth. Soy sauce in the fifth. The sixth waits.
Bring the large pan of water to a rolling boil. Her noodles go in for three minutes, then you drain them into the colander with her well back.
Turn the noodles through a splash of oil, ladle cooking water into the sixth bowl for anyone wanting broth, and share them between the 4 dinner bowls.
Everybody builds their own on top of the noodles she cut. Forks, or chopsticks for whoever fancies the fight.
second.tip: Fresh noodles cook in the time it takes to lay the table. Fish one out at two minutes and let her bite it.

alternatives: Store-bought noodles, and she runs the whole topping bar.
Toppings only, over rice or toast.
Freeze the spare noodles in nests for the week.
Lay the table for four, one job at a time.
outAgain: A train ride, two stops out and two back
Indoor playground, for a Saturday spent standing still
The park in the last of the light
A café, and she orders her own
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 17 months and eats what everyone else eats, so chop a few noodles short for him and add carrot ribbons and egg to his tray. Nothing hot goes down in front of him. On the train he wants the window and the word for it, and train go may arrive today.

insight.headline: Laying the track is planning, and it's harder than driving on it.
paras: Everything Azlyn did this morning paid off at one o'clock. Nothing about rolling and cutting fed her at the time, and a three-year-old lives close to the present, so holding a plan across four hours is real work for her. She manages it here because the plan hangs over a chair back where she can see it. Children this age keep an intention alive through a physical reminder long before they can hold one in their heads. Say at breakfast what one o'clock is for, point at the drying nests when she asks about lunch, and the waiting teaches on its own.

days.safety: A full pan of boiling water and the steam coming off the colander. Steam scalds worse than the water does, so she stands back for the drain and Kreston is out of the kitchen entirely while the pan moves. Raw egg dough goes in the trash, not in a mouth.

days.title: Beating Air Into It
days.prepTonight: Stand four eggs out so they reach room temperature, and mix a jar of bubbles: warm water, a squeeze of dish soap, a spoon of sugar.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Whisk and the Empty Bowl

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Bath and the Sunday Book Pile

opening.title: Separating the Yolks
opening.need: 4 eggs · 2 large bowls, one metal or glass · 1 fork.
steps: She cracks each egg on the flat of the table, never the bowl rim, and opens it into her cupped hand over the metal bowl.
The white runs between her fingers and the yolk stays in her palm. It goes into the second bowl. A broken one joins the yolks and you crack another.
Beat the yolks smooth with the fork. Tell her the other bowl is the hard one and leave it until 9:15.

main.title: Whisking Until It Stands Up
materials: 2 large bowls, one metal or glass
1 jam jar with a lid, the substitute if there is no whisk
steps: Give the yolks she separated at 8:00 one more turn of the fork, cover that bowl with the dish towel and stand it in the fridge. Two of them go into the batter at 1:00.
Pinch of salt over the whites. She whisks while you count sixty, then you take sixty, then her again. With no whisk in the house, the whites go in the jam jar with the lid on and she shakes.
Stop at the loose foam stage. Lift the whisk out and show her the trail it leaves in the surface, then hand it straight back.
Once the foam turns white and holds a mark, rain the tablespoon of sugar in while somebody keeps whisking.
Pull the whisk up and look at the peak. A tip that flops needs more. A tip that stands is done, and it takes longer than either of you expects.
Hold the bowl upside down over her head. Nothing lands on her, and she will ask for that eleven times.
main.tip: Any grease kills it. Wipe both bowls dry and keep every scrap of yolk out of the whites. Ten minutes with no thickening means starting again.

outside.title: Bubbles in the Cold Air
paras: Bubbles are strange at the end of November. Cold air makes them slow and heavy, so they sink and sit on the grass instead of sailing off. Blow a few low over the frost and see how long one lasts on a cold leaf. She chases them.

days.infant: Kreston is 17 months and tracks a bubble right across the yard now, head and eyes together. Give him his own bowl and a spoon on the kitchen floor for the whisking hour. He is two-word building, so feed him more bubble outside, over and over, and wait for him to have a go at it.

second.title: The Pancakes That Puff
second.intro: The bowl of whites goes into batter, and what comes out of the pan stands twice as tall.
steps: Flour, baking powder and the pinch of salt into the large mixing bowl. She stirs the dry lot together with her hand.
Well in the middle, same as yesterday. The 2 egg yolks in, then the milk in a thin stream while she stirs outward.
One ladle of the whisked egg whites in first, stirred through hard to loosen the batter.
The rest go in with a lift and a fold, under and over, no stirring. Show her once. She will stir anyway, so let her flatten half of it.
Butter or oil in the nonstick skillet over medium heat. She ladles the batter in from the side with your hand over hers.
Once the bubbles on top open and stay open, you turn each one with the spatula. She counts them out loud.
Stack them on the 4 plates with honey or jam, holding one up sideways so she sees the depth.
second.tip: Use as few strokes as you can manage. Every extra stir knocks out air she spent an hour putting in.

alternatives: Ordinary pancakes, and she does the ladling.
Whisk cream instead and watch it go past soft into butter.
Fold the whites into the batter and bake the lot as one tray pancake.
Keep the whites cold and make them tomorrow.
outAgain: A sunset walk, out at three, because the light goes at half past four
The duck pond, then home before it goes dark
A friend's house with a plate of pancakes
Round the block on the scooter
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 17 months and feeds himself a wedge of pancake, so tear one into strips and leave the honey off his. On the sunset walk he wants to be down and walking, which is slow, so allow twice the time and take the stroller for the way home.

insight.headline: Air is invisible, and she needs to feel it push before she'll believe in it.
paras: Four egg whites weigh nothing much and end up filling half a bowl, with nothing added but her arm. Children treat air as absence until something makes it act like a substance, and this morning it lifted a bowl's worth of foam over her own head. Preschoolers who get a physical demonstration of air taking up room start using it to explain other things: bubbles, balloons, the bread rising, wind against a coat. The demonstration has to be one she performed herself, which this was. She will bring it up again this week in an odd place, and that is the idea traveling.

days.safety: Raw egg. She washes her hands after cracking and nobody licks the bowl, Kreston included. Hot fat spits the moment batter hits it, so she ladles from the side with your hand over hers and the pan handle turned in.

days.title: One Cup Means One Cup
days.prepTonight: Stand the butter out to soften, put the scale and the muffin pan on the table, and decide which low cupboard is coming out this afternoon.

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: Carrying the Plates to the Table

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Bath, Then the Muffin She Saved

opening.title: Filling the Cup Four Ways
opening.need: 1 measuring cup or a mug · rice, water, sugar and cotton balls · 1 tray.
steps: Fill the same cup four times over the tray: rice, water, sugar, cotton balls, all to the same line. She does the pouring and the stuffing.
Ask which cupful is heaviest. Let her lift each one and change her mind twice.
Tell her the cup holds the same amount every time whatever goes in it, and leave that sitting there. She tests it at 9:15 with flour.

main.title: Two Trays, One Guessed
materials: 2 cups self-rising flour (250 g), or all-purpose flour plus 2 tsp baking powder
7 tbsp oil (100 ml), or 7 tbsp soft butter (100 g)
Kitchen scale or a measuring cup
steps: Two bowls. She writes 1 on one sticky label and 2 on the other with the pen and sticks them on.

Bowl one, measured together: half the flour, half the sugar, half the oil or butter, one egg, half the milk. She reads the scale or fills the measuring cup to the line, and levels every tablespoon flat.
Bowl two is hers on her own. Same five things, same packets, no scale and no cup. She pours until it looks right to her. Say nothing.
Six paper liners per bowl in the muffin pan, a heaped tablespoon into each, and the labels moved onto the pan so you know which half is which.
Twenty minutes at 375°F (190°C). The pan goes in and comes out with your hands and she stays at the table while the door is open.
Cool them, then taste one from each side with whoever is in the house and take a vote.
main.tip: Hers may win, and if it does, say so. Measuring is how you make the same thing twice.

outside.title: Heavy Pocket, Light Pocket
paras: One coat pocket for heavy, one for light, one thing at a time. Stones, a wet fir cone and a lump of frozen mud go one side. Dry leaves, a feather, a seed case go the other. Walk the loop and let her feel her coat pull. Weigh both piles in her hands on the doorstep before anything comes in.

days.infant: Kreston is 17 months and carries things the whole length of a walk now. Pick him one stone wider than his fist to hold for the whole loop and see whether he still has it at the gate. He will hand it to Azlyn for her pocket, and handing over on purpose is newer than picking up.

second.title: Everything Out of One Cupboard
second.intro: One low cupboard comes out onto the floor, gets counted, and goes back in an order she decides.
materials: 1 large tray or a clear patch of floor
1 bag for anything out of date
steps: She empties the cupboard onto the tray or the clear patch of floor, one thing at a time, passing each one to you.
The shelf comes up with the damp cloth. She does the flat middle and you do the corners.
Sorting is hers: cans, packets, jars, and a pile for whatever refuses to be any of those. Count each group and write the numbers on the paper.
Read the dates together. Anything gone over goes into the out-of-date bag and she carries it to the trash.
Three things nobody in this house is ever going to eat go into the food bank bag, and she picks them.
She decides where each group goes back, and the heavy cans go low because she has to lift them.
One sticky note per group, drawn with the marker and stuck inside the door, so tomorrow she puts things away without asking.
second.tip: Ninety minutes sounds long for one cupboard. She counts the cans twice, stacks them four ways, and runs the clock out on her own.

alternatives: One shelf instead of the whole cupboard.
Sort the cans by size, then by picture, then by weight.
Pack the food bank bag and stop there.
outAgain: The hill walk, up the steep side with the muffins in a bag
The riverside path, flat, for legs that have been up and down all afternoon
The green space with a ball
The corner store, and she carries the milk
days.krestonPM: Keep Kreston clear while the cupboard is open, then give him three empty packets and a shelf of his own. At 17 months he puts things in and takes them out for ten or fifteen minutes, then comes back to it three times. On the hill he wants carrying at the steep part and walking at the top, which is the wrong way round for your back.

insight.headline: Pumping a tire is the first time she'll feel her own strength do something useful.
paras: A bike pump is the usual version of this. Today it is a cupboard, emptied and put back by her arms, with the cans going on the low shelf because that is what she can lift. Children work out what they are capable of from jobs where the effort is theirs and the result stays visible afterwards, and a real household task does that in a way a toy cannot. Effort she can feel is the part that registers. She will open that cupboard tomorrow and see her own decisions in it. Give her the heavy end of things more often than feels necessary.

days.safety: The oven and the hot pan are yours alone, and she stays at the table while the door is open. Cans come out of the cupboard one at a time and never stack where they can come down on her feet. Cotton balls, fir cones, seed cases and small stones are all the size Kreston chokes on at 17 months, so none of them go to him, the collecting pockets stay on Azlyn's coat, the only stone he carries is the wide one you picked, and both walk piles get weighed on the doorstep and left outside. Count the cotton balls out of the bag and back into it, and sweep the floor before he is down. Keep Kreston behind a gate while the cupboard is on the floor, and the out-of-date bag goes straight out to the trash rather than standing by the door.

days.title: Taste It and Fix It
days.prepTonight: Put five small bowls out with salt, sugar, dried herbs, pepper and a splash of vinegar in them, cover them with a plate, and find the can opener.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: Pitchers, Funnels and a Tray of Oats

opening.title: One Pinch at a Time
opening.need: the five covered bowls · 1 saucer · 1 glass of water.
steps: Uncover the five bowls you set out last night, salt, sugar, dried herbs, pepper and vinegar, and let her smell each one with her eyes shut. Name them as she goes.
A pinch of each onto the saucer, licked off a wet fingertip with a swig of water in between. She pulls a face at the vinegar and goes back to it twice.
Ask her which one she would put in food. Take the answer as it comes and tell her the bowl she is fixing arrives at 9:15.

main.title: Fixing the Boring Bowl
materials: 1 can chopped tomatoes, or 2 boiled potatoes mashed with water
Small bowls of salt, sugar, dried herbs, lemon juice or vinegar, black pepper
steps: Tomatoes into the bowl, or the two mashed potatoes loosened with water. She tastes it plain. Write her first word for it at the top of the paper.
The five small bowls go in a row with a teaspoon standing in each. The sixth spoon is hers for tasting and it gets rinsed between goes.
One thing, one pinch, stir, taste, then a mouthful of water from the pitcher. She chooses the bowl every time and you write down the order.
Keep going while she is interested. Leave the sugar alone even when she puts three lots in, because that is a result too.
Overdone is repairable. A splash from the pitcher pulls it back, and she does the fixing.
Read the list back in order, then dip bread in it and let everyone at the table taste what she built.
main.tip: Keep your face still. She reads you between spoonfuls, and one wince ends the experiment faster than the vinegar does.

outside.title: Following the Cooking Smells
paras: Cold air carries cooking a long way. Walk toward whatever you can smell and name the door it came out of: the bakery, the takeout place, coffee, woodsmoke off a chimney. She points before you do. On the way home ask which smell she would eat and which one she would only stand near.

days.infant: Kreston is 17 months and pulls a face at sour things, so give him the smelling and none of the tasting. Hold each bowl under his nose for a second. Vinegar gets a whole-body reaction and he asks for it again, a joke he is old enough to be in on.

second.title: Pitchers, Funnels and a Tray of Oats
second.intro: Ninety minutes that ask nothing of you. Set it up, sit down beside it, and let her pour.
materials: A handful of large dried pasta shapes
1 funnel, or the top half of a cut plastic bottle
steps: Deep tray or dishpan on the table, never the floor. All the oats in, and the pasta shapes stirred through by hand.
Hand her the two pitchers and nothing else for the first ten minutes. Pouring between two containers is the whole game and she runs it herself.
Add the funnel, or the cut bottle top. Show her once that a pitcher fills a yogurt cup faster through it, then leave her alone.
The sieve next. Oats fall through and the pasta stays behind, and she will do that eight times before she says anything about it.
Three yogurt cups and the ladle. Count the ladlefuls out loud and see how many fill one cup.
Sweep between rounds with the dustpan and brush. She does the sweeping and it counts as part of the play.
Bag the oats at the end. They keep, and the tray comes out again in the bad weeks.
second.tip: Say nothing for the first ten minutes. Every suggestion shortens the run, and a tray like this holds her twenty minutes at a stretch, twice over, if nobody organizes it.

alternatives: Warm water in the dishpan instead of oats.
Dried pasta only, and she sorts it by shape.
Pour in the bath tonight and skip the sweeping.
Two pitchers, one sink, one dish towel.
outAgain: Swimming
Indoor playground if the pool is closed for cleaning
The library, for a book about food
Home, with the tray again, on a week that has been long
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 17 months and swims by holding on and kicking hard, so take him under the arms and let his legs work. He kicks a ball on land now and the same movement turns up here. Twenty minutes, then out and warm before he goes quiet on you.

insight.headline: Finishing a week by using everything she made beats one more new thing.
paras: This afternoon is a game she has played since she could sit up, with one new piece in it, the funnel. Familiar hands leave her attention free for the part that is new, which is why the second and third go at something teach more than the first. The same rule runs the rest of the week. On Thursday she cooks a dinner out of things she has already made, and none of it will be unfamiliar enough to frighten her. Repeating with a small change is how a three-year-old consolidates, and it looks like nothing much from the outside.

days.safety: Oats and dried pasta end up on the floor, and Kreston at 17 months puts everything in his mouth. Sweep between rounds and keep the tray on the table, not the floor. Salt as well: she is tasting pinch after pinch today, so keep the bowls small, and Kreston gets none of it. The pepper bowl gets the smallest pinch of the five, and it goes onto food rather than onto her tongue if it catches her throat. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: Her Own Kit
days.prepTonight: Move the puff pastry from the freezer to the fridge, and settle tonight which low drawer becomes hers in the morning.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Bath and the Cheese Straw She Kept

opening.title: Emptying the Bottom Drawer
opening.need: the low drawer · 1 tray or a clear counter · 1 trash bag.
steps: Tell her the drawer is hers from today and then let her empty it. Everything comes out onto the tray or the counter, one handful at a time.
Go through the pile with her: what belongs to the kitchen, what belongs upstairs, what belongs in the trash bag. She rules on each one.
Leave the drawer standing open and empty. She will look at it four times before 9:15.

main.title: What Goes in Her Drawer
materials: 1 low drawer or cupboard shelf she can reach
1 hook or peg for her apron, with screws and a screwdriver, or adhesive pads
Card and a marker for the label
steps: She wipes the empty drawer out with the damp cloth, corners and all, and dries it with her hand.
Lay seven things on the table: the pitcher, the bowl, the butter knife, the wooden spoon, the small whisk, the sieve and the dish towel. She handles each one and decides where it lives in the drawer.
The eighth is hers to choose off this morning's pile. Take whatever she picks, a lid or a muffin liner included.
Stick or screw the hook on the end of the unit at her height and hang her apron on it.
Card and marker: she draws the label for the front. Ask what it says and write her words underneath in your handwriting.
Shut it, open it, and let her unpack and repack the lot twice while you stand there doing nothing.
main.tip: Nothing goes in that drawer without her say-so from today, and nothing comes out of it without asking her. The rule lasts longer than the drawer does.

outside.title: What the Frost Got
paras: First of December, and the frost has been through the yard. Walk her round the things it flattened: the blackened dahlia, the collapsed nasturtium, the soft edge on a fallen leaf. Then find what shrugged it off: the ivy, the holly, the grass and her rosemary bush. Break the ice out of a bucket or a bird bath in one sheet and let her carry it in gloves until the cold comes through them.

days.infant: Kreston is 17 months and copies whatever job is going, so give him the second cloth and a low cupboard door to wipe while Azlyn does her drawer. He stays in the room through the hook, which is what the adhesive pads are for. He wipes one spot for a long time. Outside, put the ice sheet flat on the grass and let him stamp on it in boots.

second.title: Cheese Straws, Two Tins
second.intro: Two trays go in and only one stays in this house. She decides who gets the other one before she starts twisting.
materials: 1 sheet ready-rolled puff pastry, or 1 2/3 cups flour (200 g) rubbed into 7 tbsp butter (100 g) with 4 tbsp water
1 small bowl and 1 fork for beating it
steps: Ask who the second tin is for and let her name somebody. A neighbor, the woman at playgroup, whoever she says.
Unroll the pastry onto parchment paper, or roll the rubbed-in dough out with the rolling pin until it is as thick as her finger.
She beats the egg and paints it over the top with the pastry brush or the back of a teaspoon, edges included.
All the grated cheese scattered on by her, then pressed down with one pass of the rolling pin so it stays put.
She cuts long strips with her butter knife out of her drawer, holds each end, and twists. They come out wonky and bake fine.
Twelve minutes at 400°F (200°C) on the two lined baking trays. You open the oven and move the trays, she stays at the table.
Cooled, they split between the tin and the paper bag. She carries the bag herself and hands it over.
second.tip: Twisting is a two-handed job going opposite ways, which is hard at three. Hold one end for her until she asks you to stop.

alternatives: Straight straws, no twist, and double the cheese.
Cut the pastry into shapes with a cup rim instead.
Bake one tray and freeze the other for a rough day.
Draw a card for the person getting the bag.
outAgain: Indoor playground, the quiet weekday session, before school lets out
The library, and she can take her label idea for a book about cooking
The park, boots on, for whatever is left of the ice
Round to whoever the paper bag is for
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 17 months and kicks a ball with a proper swing now, so the quiet indoor playground session is the right one: room to run and nobody knocking him over. Give him a corner of cheese straw at snack time, broken small. He wants his own bag to carry and any bag will do.

insight.headline: The moon changing shape is the first thing she'll notice that she can't touch.
paras: Azlyn learns objects by acting on them, and today she got a drawer, a hook and a tin she can carry. The moon offers her none of that. She will point at it from the bathroom window this week, tell you it followed the car, and notice two weeks later that the shape is wrong. Watching a thing change that she cannot lift or fix is a different kind of thinking, and it is where patience over weeks starts. Nothing about the moon rewards her for hurrying, and that is new to her. Answer her questions about it straight, and say when you have no idea.

days.safety: The hot oven and the trays are adult hands only, and Azlyn stays at the table while the door is open. She washes her hands after the raw egg, and none of it goes near Kreston. Gloves go on before she lifts the ice, and it comes off her hands the moment they sting. Keep Kreston off the ice sheet unless it is lying on grass. The screws and the screwdriver both go back in your pocket between turns on the hook, and you check the floor before Kreston is loose in the room, because a screw is pincer-grip size at 17 months. Use the adhesive pads if he is in the kitchen with you.

days.title: The Dinner Is Hers
days.prepTonight: Cut six cards out of a cereal box with your scissors and leave them on the table with the marker, and move her noodles from the freezer to the fridge.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: From the Pan to the Plates

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Bath and the Cookbook She Started

opening.title: The Menu on the Fridge
steps: Tell her tonight's dinner is hers to cook and watch what her face does with that.
She draws the menu: what is in it, who is eating, and a dessert. Write her words beside each drawing without tidying them.
Stick it on the fridge with the magnet at her eye level. Everyone who comes in the kitchen today gets told about it.

main.title: Six Jobs on Six Cards
materials: 6 index cards, or 6 pieces cut from a cereal box
1 piece of hard cheese for grating
steps: Six cards, one picture each in marker: a tap, a leaf, a peeler, a knife, a grater, a cup. She draws what she can. Lay them face up in a row with the six small trays behind them.
Card one: everything washed in the bowl of water onto the first tray. The card moves to the done pile.
Card two: salad torn onto the second tray, by hand, into pieces she thinks are the right size.
Card three: she holds the carrot flat on the cutting board while you take the skin off in ribbons with the vegetable peeler. Third tray.
Cards four and five: soft vegetables cut with her butter knife onto the fourth tray, then cheese grated onto the fifth, you holding the grater down and her pushing.
Card six: oil and vinegar in the measuring cups, tipped into the biggest one and whisked, then poured into the jam jar with the lid on. It stands by the plates until dinner.
main.tip: Let her run the card order herself, even backwards. She turns six loose jobs into a sequence she can see.

outside.title: The Same Trees, Bare Again
paras: Walk the route you walked on New Year's Day. The trees are back where they started, bare and structural. Stand under the biggest one and take a picture to sit beside January's. Ask what it looked like in the summer and see how much of that she has kept.

days.infant: Kreston is 17 months and wants a job when he sees one going, so give him the sixth tray and one washed carrot to carry to the table. He drops it once. He walked none of this route in January and manages most of it now.

second.title: From the Pan to the Plates
second.intro: Six trays of prepped food and a menu on the fridge. She cooks, and the house sits down hungry.
materials: The menu from this morning, on the fridge
Her noodles, a muffin and the last of her cheese straws from earlier in the week, or whatever is in the fridge
steps: She lines the trays along the counter in the order things go in, checking the menu on the fridge for anything missing.
Fill the large pan, set it on the back burner with the handle in, and put her step at the side of the stovetop rather than in front.
Her noodles go in at the boil. She stirs with the wooden spoon and your hand stays over hers the whole time.
Cut vegetables in for the last two minutes. She counts them down out loud from twenty.
Lift some out with the tasting spoon and cool it. The salt shaker is hers: one pinch, taste again, and she says when it is right.
Oven mitts on you. The pan comes off the heat and drains into the colander, then the noodles go back in the pan on the folded dish towel, and the pan goes into the fridge until six.
At six you warm it through and she ladles onto the four plates. She carries the salad tray, the muffin and the cheese straws over, you carry the four hot plates, and everybody eats what she made.
second.tip: Give her the ladle and let the plates come out uneven. Whatever nobody finishes goes into a covered bowl with her name on it, and she serves it again tomorrow.

alternatives: She plates up a cold dinner and skips the stovetop.
One job at the stovetop, and you do the rest.
Set the table and count out everything for four, ready for six o'clock.
Photograph each tray and start the cookbook with that.
outAgain: The pharmacy, then the park bench with a snack before the light goes
The market for one thing she chooses for tomorrow
Round the block with a flashlight each
The library, for a book about something she cooked this week
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 17 months and eats what she cooked, cut small and cooled on his tray. Behind the gate while the pan moves, out again the second it is down. On the bench he wants to be off it kicking a stone along the path, so build in the extra fifteen minutes.

insight.headline: Distance is the part of space that nobody tells her about.
paras: Somebody teaches her colors, numbers and shapes, and nobody sits her down about how far away things are. Her own judgment of it is still rough. Children this age will try to climb into a toy car or reach a thing well past their arm, because a body that keeps changing recalibrates size and distance every few weeks. That is why today's stovetop rule is about where her feet go rather than about being careful. Walking the January route again gives her the other half of it, distance measured in her own steps, which is the version she can feel.

days.safety: She is at the stovetop as the cook for the first time. Handles turn in, the pan base stays hotter than it looks long after it comes off, and she carries the salad tray while you carry the four hot plates. Kreston is strapped in or behind the gate the whole time pans are moving.
